A responsive, accessible reference organized by grape composition, fermentation, aging, and spoilage.

Compounds present in the berry before fermentation. Skin, pulp,
seeds, juice. These vary by variety, terroir, and ripeness of the
grape.

Primary fermentable sugars (150–250 g/L). Converted to ethanol +
CO₂.

Dominant stable acid (2000–8000 ppm). Persists through
fermentation.

Sharp acid decreases with ripeness. Converted to lactic acid during
MLF.

Key terpene in Muscat/Riesling. Threshold ~15 ppb. Bound forms
released in aging.

Norisoprenoid; threshold ~0.05 ppb. Potentiates all other fruit
aromas.

From β-carotene. Threshold ~0.007 ppb. Hallmark of Cabernet
Sauvignon.

Threshold ~2 ppb. Cool-climate marker. Destroyed by UV light and
sunlight.

Red pigments in skins (50 mg/L Pinot → 5 g/L Tannat). Stabilize
during aging.

Main astringency source (0.5–4 g/L red wine). Polymerize and soften
with age.

Odorless precursors to potent thiols (3MH, 4MMP). Released by yeast
enzymes.

Antioxidant tripeptide protecting varietal thiols from oxidative
browning.

Minor acid; consumed by LAB during MLF, generating diacetyl + acetic
acid.

Saccharomyces cerevisiae: Converts sugars to ethanol + CO₂ while
generating hundreds of secondary metabolites that define the wine’s aromatic backbone

Primary product (80,000–160,000 ppm). Solvent, preservative, and
aroma carrier.

3rd most abundant after water and ethanol. Contributes body and
mouthfeel.

Key acetate ester. Threshold ~0.03 mg/L. Higher at cool fermentation
temps.

Most abundant ester. Fault above ~120 mg/L. Produced by yeast and
bacteria.

Fruity ethyl esters; threshold ~0.005–0.02 mg/L. Decrease with
bottle age.

Most abundant fusel alcohol. Harsh above 300–400 mg/L. From leucine
catabolism.
Pleasant fusel alcohol from phenylalanine. Threshold ~10 mg/L.

Main aldehyde. Binds SO₂. High levels signal oxidation. Up to 500
ppm in Sherry.

Butter aroma. Threshold 0.2 mg/L (white), 1 mg/L (red). Produced by
yeast + LAB.

Main non-volatile yeast acid (500–1500 ppm). Unique
salty-bitter-sour taste.
Volatile acidity. Fault above 0.9 g/L (white) / 1.2 g/L (red).

Potent varietal thiols released by yeast. 4MMP threshold ~1 ppb; 3MH
~60 ppb.

Reductive faults from N-deficient fermentation. Removed by aeration
or Cu treatment.

Yeast cell wall polysaccharides. Improve mouthfeel and tartrate/foam
stability.

Oenococcus oeni: converts malic acid → lactic acid + CO₂. Transforms
acidity, texture and aromatic complexity.

Core MLF reaction. Raises pH by 0.1–0.3 units. Softens overall acid
profile.

Key MLF aroma compound. Can spike to 5+ mg/L during MLF. From citric
acid + pyruvate.

Diacetyl reduction product. Threshold ~150 mg/L — usually
sub-threshold.

Further acetoin reduction. Non-aromatic; contributes marginally to
body.

Lactic acid + ethanol. Accumulates slowly post-MLF. Adds textural
softness.

From citric acid catabolism by LAB. Higher risk with elevated citric
acid in must.

Decarboxylation of amino acids by LAB. EU guideline <10 mg/L for
histamine.

Raises pH 0.1–0.3 units. Affects SO₂ efficacy, color, and microbial
stability.

Oak extraction, oxidation, tannin evolution, and slow reductive
chemistry over months to decades in barrel and bottle.

Oak lignin breakdown. Threshold ~0.1 mg/L. American > French oak.
Decreases with reuse.

Oak phenylpropanoid. Threshold ~0.5 mg/L. Higher in American oak
barrels.

From toasted oak lignin. Threshold ~0.065–0.095 mg/L. Heavier toast
= more.

Hallmark of American oak. cis-isomer threshold ~0.067 mg/L. French
oak: trace only.

Hemicellulose degradation during toasting. Usually below sensory
threshold (~14 mg/L).

Water-soluble oak tannins. Enable micro-oxygenation and modulate
astringency.

Oxidative aging marker. Threshold ~7 ppb. Defines Sherry, Vin Jaune,
Madeira character.

Develops in Riesling over 10–30 years. Threshold ~20 ppb. Prized by
collectors.

Stable pigments from anthocyanins + pyruvate/acetaldehyde. Brick-red
hues in aged reds.

Tannin-anthocyanin coupling via oxidation or acetaldehyde bridging.
Stabilize color.

Increases slowly in bottle from SMM hydrolysis. Adds umami below ~25
ppb threshold.

Released during yeast autolysis on lees. Key to Champagne foam
stability and mouthfeel.

Unwanted organisms produce characteristic fault compounds
Brettanomyces, acetic acid bacteria, aberrant LAB, and chemical
faults

Primary Brett compound. Threshold 140–440 ppb. From p-coumaric acid.
Very persistent.

Co-occurs with 4-EP (~10:1 ratio). Threshold ~33 ppb. From ferulic
acid via Brett.

Brett and LAB product. Threshold ~0.4–1 mg/L. Persistent; very
difficult to mask.

Acetobacter oxidizes ethanol. Fault above 0.9 g/L (white) / 1.2 g/L
(red). Legal limits apply.

Accompanies high VA. Fault threshold ~120 mg/L. Legal limit
typically 150 mg/L.

Threshold ~1.4 ppb. Sub-threshold levels suppress aroma perception.
Most common wine fault.

Only perceived after saliva raises pH. Common in low-sulfite natural
wines.

LAB fructose reduction in stuck/high-sugar musts. Fault in dry wines
— syrupy sweetness.

Sorbic acid metabolized by LAB → 2-ethoxyhexa-3,5-diene. Threshold
~0.1 mg/L.

Gluconobacter product in damaged/botrytised fruit. Strong SO₂
binder. Signals compromised fruit.
